questions.q: Define a virus and state the two types of nucleic acid it can contain.
questions.a: A virus is a non-cellular, obligate intracellular parasite consisting of a nucleic acid core (either DNA or RNA, never both) surrounded by a protein capsid. The two types of nucleic acid are DNA and RNA. A wrong answer (e.g., "viruses contain both DNA and RNA" or "viruses are cellular") reveals the student hasn't grasped the fundamental acellular nature and the mutual exclusivity of viral genetic material — a critical distinction from cellular organisms.

questions.q: Why are viruses considered non-living outside a host cell but living inside? Explain using two specific criteria of life.
questions.a: Outside a host, viruses are inert crystals: they lack metabolism, cannot reproduce independently, and show no response to stimuli — failing criteria of metabolism and autonomous reproduction. Inside a host, they hijack ribosomes, ATP, and enzymes to replicate their genome and synthesise proteins, exhibiting reproduction and metabolism (albeit borrowed). A wrong answer focusing only on "they replicate" without mentioning host-dependence shows confusion between autonomous life processes and parasitic replication.

questions.q: A new plant pathogen is discovered. It passes through filters that retain viruses, consists only of low-molecular-weight circular ssRNA, and lacks a protein coat. Identify it as a virus or viroid and justify.
questions.a: It is a viroid. Step 1: Filterability smaller than viruses indicates size < viruses. Step 2: Composition is only RNA — no protein coat (capsid) means it cannot be a virus. Step 3: Circular ssRNA of low molecular weight matches Diener's discovery of potato spindle tuber viroid. A wrong answer identifying it as a virus reveals inability to apply the defining structural difference: viruses always have a capsid, viroids never do.

questions.q: Compare the structural symmetry and genetic material of Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) and Bacteriophage. How does this relate to their hosts?
questions.a: TMV: helical symmetry, single-stranded RNA (plant virus). Bacteriophage: polyhedral head with helical tail, double-stranded DNA (bacterial virus). Plant viruses typically have ssRNA and helical/rod shapes; bacteriophages have dsDNA and complex polyhedral+tail structures for injecting DNA into bacteria. A wrong answer swapping genetic material types (e.g., TMV has DNA) shows failure to link nucleic acid type to host kingdom — a pattern NCERT explicitly states.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Since viruses replicate and evolve, they should be placed in a separate kingdom in Whittaker's classification." Provide two reasons against this.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. Reason 1: Whittaker's criteria require cell structure (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), body organisation, and mode of nutrition — viruses lack all three (acellular, no organisation, no nutrition). Reason 2: Viruses are obligate parasites with no metabolic machinery; they cannot be classified as autotrophs, heterotrophs, or saprotrophs. A wrong answer agreeing reveals misunderstanding that classification is based on cellular organisation, not just replication ability.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to prove that the infectious agent of potato spindle tuber disease is RNA-only and lacks protein.
questions.a: Extract sap from infected plants. Treat one portion with protease (degrades protein) and another with RNase (degrades RNA). Inoculate healthy plants: protease-treated sap remains infectious (protein not needed), RNase-treated sap loses infectivity (RNA essential). This mirrors Diener's 1971 experiment. A poor answer suggesting only filtration or heat treatment shows inability to design a controlled biochemical test targeting specific macromolecules.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Viruses are non-cellular, obligate ______ parasites consisting of a nucleic acid core (either DNA or RNA, never both) enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid made of capsomeres; they are inert outside a host cell and replicate only by hijacking host machinery.
Fill in the blank: Think about the last time you had a common cold or flu — you felt sick, but the doctor said ______ won't work.
What is Viruses? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Viruses are non-cellular, obligate intracellular parasites consisting of a nucleic acid core (either DNA or RNA, never both) enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid made of capsomeres; they are inert outside a host cell and replicate only by hijacking host machinery.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Viruses?
questions.a: Students often think viruses are "alive" because they replicate and evolve, ignoring that replication is entirely host-dependent and they lack any metabolic pathway (no ATP synthesis, no ribosomes).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can explain why viruses are considered non-living outside host cells but exhibit living characteristics inside, differentiate viruses from viroids based on structural components (capsid presence/absence) and genetic material, and describe the structural symmetry of TMV (helical) and bacteriophage (polyhedral with tail).
